Natural parametrization of percolation interface and pivotal points

Nina Holden ††thanks: Institute for Theoretical Studies, ETH Zürich. Partially supported by a fellowship from the Research Council of Norway and partially supported by Dr. Max Rössler, the Walter Haefner Foundation, and the ETH Zürich Foundation. Email: nina.holden@eth-its.ethz.ch.    Xinyi Li ††thanks: Beijing International Center for Mathematical Research, Peking University. Research supported by NSFC (No. 12071012) and the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2020YFA0712900).

Abstract

We prove that the interface of critical site percolation on the triangular lattice converges to SLE6\SLE_{6} in its natural parametrization, where the discrete interface is parametrized such that each edge is crossed in one unit of time, while the limiting curve is parametrized by its 7/47/4-dimensional Minkowski content. We also prove that the scaling limit of counting measure on the pivotal points, which was proved to exist by Garban, Pete, and Schramm (2013), is its 3/43/4-dimensional Minkowski content up to a deterministic multiplicative constant.

Nous montrons que l’interface de la percolation du site critique sur le réseau triangulaire converge vers la courbe SLE6\SLE_{6} dans sa parmétrisation naturelle, où l’interface discrète est paramétrée de telle sorte que chaque arête se croise en une unité de temps, tandis que la courbe limite est paramétrée par son contenu 7/47/4-dimensionnel de Minkowski. Nous montrons également que la limite d’échelle de la mesure de comptage sur les points pivots, dont l’existence a été confirmée par Garban, Pete et Schramm (2013), est son contenu 3/43/4-dimensionnel de Minkowski jusqu’à une constante multiplicative déterministe.

1 Introduction

Percolation is one of the most studied statistical mechanics models in probability. Since the breakthrough works of Smirnov [Smi01], who proved the conformal invariance of critical site percolation on the triangular lattice, and of Schramm [Sch00], who introduced the Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE), the understanding of the scaling limit of percolation on planar lattices has greatly improved.

Garban, Pete, and Schramm [GPS13, GPS10, GPS18] made important contributions in this direction. In [GPS13] they proved scaling limit results for several important classes of points for critical percolation, including pivotal points and points on the percolation interface. They proved that the limiting measures are conformally covariant, and that they are measurable with respect to the scaling limit of percolation.

In the continuum, a substantial effort has been made to understand natural measures on special points of SLEκ curves. For example, SLEκ curves have non-trivial 2∧(1+κ/8)2\wedge(1+\kappa/8)-dimensional Minkowski content, which defines a parametrization of the curve called the natural parametrization. SLE with its natural parametrization is uniquely characterized by conformal invariance and domain Markov property, with the constraint that the parametrization is rescaled in a covariant way under the application of a conformal map. See [LS11, LZ13, LR15]. SLE with its natural parametrization is believed to describe the scaling limit of curves in statistical physics models parametrized such that one edge/face/vertex is visited in one unit of time. This conjecture was proved for the case of the loop-erased random walk (LERW) and SLE2 by Lawler and Viklund [LV16, LV17].

In this paper, we link the limiting measures in [GPS13] with the natural measures on special points of SLE6\SLE_{6}. The purpose of building the link is two-fold:

  1. 1.

    It makes the limiting measures in [GPS13] more intrinsic and concrete. In the case of percolation pivotal points, this link is important for the work of the first and third authors on the conformal embedding of uniform triangulations [HS19].

  2. 2.

    It allows us to prove that the percolation interface converges to SLE6\SLE_{6} in its natural parametrization.

1.1 The scaling limit of the percolation interface under its natural parametrization

Let us briefly recall the definition of SLE. Fix κ>0\kappa>0, and let (Bt)t≥0(B_{t})_{t\geq 0} be a standard linear Brownian motion. Consider the Loewner differential equation

∂tgt​(z)=2gt​(z)−κ​Bt,g0​(z)=z,∀z∈ℍ¯.\partial_{t}g_{t}(z)=\frac{2}{g_{t}(z)-\sqrt{\kappa}B_{t}},\qquad g_{0}(z)=z,\;\forall z\in\overline{\mathbb{H}}.

Then for each z∈ℍz\in\mathbb{H}, gt​(z)g_{t}(z) is well-defined up to some time τz∈[0,∞]\tau_{z}\in[0,\infty]. Let Kt={z:τz<t}¯K_{t}=\overline{\{z:\tau_{z}<t\}}. Then a.s. there exists a unique continuous non-self-crossing curve γ\gamma such that KtK_{t} is the closure of points disconnected from ∞\infty on ℍ\mathbb{H} by γ⁡([0,t])\gamma([0,t]). We call γ\gamma the chordal SLEκ\SLE_{\kappa} on ℍ\mathbb{H} from 00 to ∞\infty (under the capacity parametrization). Let Ω\Omega be a simply connected domain whose set of prime ends ∂Ω{\partial}\Omega is a continuous image of a circle11 1 This is the necessary and sufficient boundary condition for the Riemann mapping from the unit disk to Ω\Omega to continuously extend to the boundary. (See e.g. [Pom92].). Let a,ba,b be two distinct points on ∂Ω{\partial}\Omega. Consider a conformal map f:ℍ→Ωf:\mathbb{H}\to\Omega with f⁡(0)=af(0)=a and f⁡(∞)=bf(\infty)=b. Although there is one degree of freedom when choosing ff, the law of f⁡(γ)f(\gamma) (viewed as a continuous curve modulo increasing reparametrizations) does not depend on this choice. We call this probability measure the chordal SLEκ\SLE_{\kappa} on Ω\Omega from aa to bb, or simply SLEκ\SLE_{\kappa} on (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b).

Let 𝕋\mathbb{T} denote the regular triangular lattice where each face is an equilateral triangle. For η>0\eta>0, let η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T} be 𝕋\mathbb{T} rescaled by η\eta. Each vertex on η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T} is called a site. Let η​𝕋∗\eta\mathbb{T}^{*} denote the regular hexagonal lattice dual to η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T} such that each vertex on 𝕋\mathbb{T} corresponds to a hexagonal face on η​𝕋∗\eta\mathbb{T}^{*}. Given an edge ee of η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T}, let e∗e^{*} be its dual edge in η​𝕋∗\eta\mathbb{T}^{*}. Recall that a Jordan domain is a bounded simply connected domain on ℂ\mathbb{C} whose boundary is homeomorphic to a circle. A Jordan domain DD is called a η\eta-polygon if ∂D{\partial}D lies on the lattice η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T}. A vertex vv on η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T} is called an inner vertex (resp., boundary vertex) of DD if v∈Dv\in D (resp., v∈∂Dv\in{\partial}D). We similarly define boundary/inner edges of DD.

Suppose Ω\Omega is a Jordan domain. Let Ωη\Omega_{\eta} be the largest η\eta-polygon whose set of inner vertices is contained in Ω\Omega and forms a connected set on η​𝕋\eta\mathbb{T}. (In case of a draw, choose Ωη\Omega_{\eta} arbitrarily from the set of largest η\eta-polygons, but note that Ωη\Omega_{\eta} will be uniquely determined for all sufficiently small η\eta.) Including all inner vertices and edges of Ωη\Omega_{\eta}, we obtain a planar graph embedded in ℂ\mathbb{C} which we call the η\eta-approximation of Ω\Omega and still denote by Ωη\Omega_{\eta}.22 2 A notion of η\eta-approximation of the Jordan domain Ω\Omega is also introduced in Definition 4.1 of [CN06], which is denoted by DηD^{\eta} in their notation. One can check that DηD_{\eta} equals the union of DηD^{\eta} and its so-called external boundary defined in [CN06, Section 4]. To distinguish with the continuum, we write the union of boundary vertices and edges of Ωη\Omega_{\eta} as Δ​Ωη\Delta\Omega_{\eta}. A path on a graph is a sequence of vertices such that each vertex is adjacent to its successor. Given two distinct boundary edges of Ωη\Omega_{\eta}, removing {e,e′}\{e,e^{\prime}\} from Δ​Ωη\Delta\Omega_{\eta} gives two paths on the boundary. We let Δe,e′​Ωη\Delta_{e,e^{\prime}}\Omega_{\eta} denote the one tracing Δ​Ωη\Delta\Omega_{\eta} counterclockwise from ee to e′e^{\prime}. Given x∈∂Ωx\in{\partial}\Omega, let xηx_{\eta} be the edge on Δ​Ωη\Delta\Omega_{\eta} closest to xx (if there is a tie, choose one arbitrarily).

A site percolation on Ωη\Omega_{\eta} is a black/white coloring of inner vertices of Ωη\Omega_{\eta}. The critical Bernoulli site percolation on Ωη\Omega_{\eta}, which we denote by Ber⁡(Ωη)\operatorname{Ber}(\Omega_{\eta}), is the uniform measure on site percolations on Ωη\Omega_{\eta}. A coloring of vertices on Δ​Ωη\Delta\Omega_{\eta} is called a boundary condition. A site percolation on Ωη\Omega_{\eta} together with a boundary condition determines a coloring of vertices on Ωη\Omega_{\eta}. The (a,b)(a,b)-boundary condition is the coloring where vertices on Δaη,bη​Ωη\Delta_{a_{\eta},b_{\eta}}\Omega_{\eta} (resp., Δbη,aη​Ωη\Delta_{b_{\eta},a_{\eta}}\Omega_{\eta}) are black (resp., white). Note that this is well-defined since we required that Ωη\Omega_{\eta} does not have any cut vertices. Given a site percolation ωη\omega_{\eta} on Ωη\Omega_{\eta} with (a,b)(a,b)-boundary condition, there is a unique path γη\gamma_{\eta} on η​𝕋∗\eta\mathbb{T}^{*} from aη∗a^{*}_{\eta} to bη∗b^{*}_{\eta}, such that each edge on the path has a white vertex on its left side and a black vertex on its right side. We call γη\gamma_{\eta} the percolation interface of ωη\omega_{\eta} on (Ωη,aη,bη)(\Omega_{\eta},a_{\eta},b_{\eta}).

Let (𝒰,d𝒰)(\mathcal{U},d_{\mathcal{U}}) denote the separable metric space of continuous curves modulo reparametrization, with the distance d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}} between curves γ1:[0,T1]→ℂ\gamma^{1}:[0,T_{1}]\to\mathbb{C} and γ2:[0,T2]→ℂ\gamma^{2}:[0,T_{2}]\to\mathbb{C} defined by

d𝒰​(γ1,γ2)=infα,β[sup0≤t≤1|γ1​(α⁡(t))−γ2​(β⁡(t))|],d_{\mathcal{U}}(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})=\inf_{\alpha,\beta}\left[\sup_{0\leq t\leq 1}\big|\gamma^{1}(\alpha(t))-\gamma^{2}(\beta(t))\big|\right], (1)

where the infimum is taken over all choices of increasing bijections α:[0,1]→[0,T1]\alpha:[0,1]\to[0,T_{1}] and β:[0,1]→[0,T2]\beta:[0,1]\to[0,T_{2}]. It is proved in [Smi01, CN07] that γη\gamma_{\eta} converges to an SLE6\SLE_{6} on (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b) for the d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}}-metric (see Theorem 2.1). Although this convergence result gives a powerful tool for analyzing large scale properties of percolation (e.g. arm exponents [SW01]), a more natural notion of convergence would be under the parametrization where γη\gamma_{\eta} traverses each edge in the same amount of time. We prove this result in Theorem 1.4 below. Before stating this result, we need the notions of Minkowski content and occupation measure.

Definition 1.1.

Given a set 𝒜⊂ℂ\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{C}, for r>0r>0, let 𝒜r={z∈ℂ:B⁡(z,r)∩𝒜≠∅}\mathcal{A}^{r}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:B(z,r)\cap\mathcal{A}\neq\emptyset\}. For d∈[0,2]d\in[0,2] we define the dd-dimensional Minkowski content of 𝒜\mathcal{A} to be the following limit, provided it exists

Minkd⁡(𝒜):=limr→0rd−2​Area⁡(𝒜r).\Mink_{d}(\mathcal{A}):=\lim_{r\to 0}r^{d-2}\Area(\mathcal{A}^{r}). (2)

If the limit does not exist, then the dd-dimensional Minkowski content of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not defined.

Definition 1.2.

Fix d∈[0,2]d\in[0,2]. Let 𝒜⊂ℂ\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{C} be a random closed set and let μ\mu be a random Borel measure on ℂ\mathbb{C}. Suppose ℙ[μ(U)=Minkd(𝒜∩U)]=1\mathbb{P}[\mu(U)=\Mink_{d}(\mathcal{A}\cap U)]=1 for each Jordan domain UU with piecewise smooth boundary. We call μ𝒜\mu_{\mathcal{A}} the occupation measure of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and say that it is (a.s.) defined by the dd-dimensional Minkowski content of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Let γ\gamma be an SLE6\SLE_{6} on (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b), where Ω\Omega is a Jordan domain with smooth boundary and a,ba,b are two distinct boundary points. Assume the parametrization of γ\gamma comes from the image of a capacity-parametrized SLE6\SLE_{6} on (ℍ,0,∞)(\mathbb{H},0,\infty) under a conformal map f:ℍ→Ωf:\mathbb{H}\to\Omega with f⁡(0)=a,f⁡(∞)=bf(0)=a,f(\infty)=b. By [LR15], we know the following.

  1. 1.

    For each t∈(0,∞]t\in(0,\infty], a.s. the 7/47/4-dimensional Minkowski content of γ⁡([0,t])\gamma([0,t]) exists and defines the occupation measure of γ⁡([0,t])\gamma([0,t]) as in Definition 1.2. We denote the occupation measure of γ⁡((,,,))\gamma((0,\infty)) by 𝔪γ\mathfrak{m}_{\gamma}.

  2. 2.

    The function t↦Mink7/4⁡(γ⁡([0,t]))t\mapsto\Mink_{7/4}\left(\gamma([0,t])\right) is a.s. strictly increasing and Hölder continuous.

Definition 1.3.

Suppose Ω\Omega is a Jordan domain with smooth boundary. Let γ\gamma be an SLE6\SLE_{6} on (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b), where a,ba,b are two distinct boundary points. Let γ^:[0,𝔪γ​(Ω)]→Ω\widehat{\gamma}:[0,\mathfrak{m}_{\gamma}(\Omega)]\to\Omega be the parametrization of γ\gamma such that Mink7/4⁡(γ⁡([0,t]))\Mink_{7/4}(\gamma([0,t])) =t=t for any t∈[0,𝔪γ​(Ω)]t\in[0,\mathfrak{m}_{\gamma}(\Omega)]. Then γ^\widehat{\gamma} is called the natural parametrization of γ\gamma.

In fact [LR15] mainly focuses on the upper half plane. However, as explained below Theorem 1.1 there, the case of Jordan domains with smooth boundary can be easily obtained by the covariance of Minkowski content under conformal mappings.

Define the following distance ρ\rho between two parametrized curves γ1:[0,T1]→ℂ\gamma^{1}:[0,T_{1}]\to\mathbb{C} and γ2:[0,T2]→ℂ\gamma^{2}:[0,T_{2}]\to\mathbb{C}.

ρ⁡(γ1,γ2)=[|T2−T1|+sup0≤s≤1|γ2​(s​T1)−γ1​(s​T2)|].\rho(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=\left[|T_{2}-T_{1}|+\sup_{0\leq s\leq 1}|\gamma^{2}(sT_{1})-\gamma^{1}(sT_{2})|\right]. (3)

As mentioned above, for statistical mechanical models where SLE is the scaling limit in the d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}}-metric, it is believed that the convergence should also hold in the ρ\rho-metric under the natural parametrization. In this paper, we prove this for the percolation interface.

Theorem 1.4.

Let (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b), γ\gamma, and γ^\widehat{\gamma} be as in Definition 1.3. For η>0\eta>0, sample ωη\omega_{\eta} from Ber⁡(Ωη)\operatorname{Ber}(\Omega_{\eta}) and let γη\gamma_{\eta} be the interface of ωη\omega_{\eta} from aηa_{\eta} to bηb_{\eta}. Pick cl>0c_{\operatorname{l}}>0, write ξη=cl​η2/α2η​(η,1)\xi_{\eta}=c_{\operatorname{l}}\eta^{2}/\alpha_{2}^{\eta}(\eta,1), and let γ^η\widehat{\gamma}_{\eta} be the parametrization of γη\gamma_{\eta} with constant speed (with respect to the Euclidean metric) such that each edge is crossed in ξη\xi_{\eta} units of time. Then with an appropriate choice of clc_{\operatorname{l}}, the curve γ^η\widehat{\gamma}_{\eta} converges weakly to γ^\widehat{\gamma} in the ρ\rho-metric.

Fix cl>0c_{\operatorname{l}}>0, and let the (normalized) interface measure τη\tau_{\eta} on γη\gamma_{\eta} be defined by

τη:=cl​∑e∈γηδe​η2α2η​(η,1),\tau_{\eta}:=c_{\operatorname{l}}\sum_{e\in\gamma_{\eta}}\delta_{e}\frac{\eta^{2}}{\alpha^{\eta}_{2}(\eta,1)}, (4)

where α2η​(η,1)\alpha^{\eta}_{2}(\eta,1) is a normalizing constant depending on η\eta that we will specify in Section 2.4, and δe\delta_{e} is the measure assigning unit mass uniformly along ee and 0 elsewhere. The following is proved in [GPS13].

Theorem 1.5 ([GPS13]).

In the setting of Theorem 1.4, there is a coupling of (ωη)η>0(\omega_{\eta})_{\eta>0} and γ\gamma such that as η→0\eta\to 0, it holds a.s. that γη\gamma_{\eta} converges to γ\gamma in the d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}}-metric, and τη\tau_{\eta} in (4) converges to a random Borel measure τ\tau supported on the range of γ\gamma in the weak topology. Moreover, τ\tau is measurable with respect to γ\gamma.

It was not proved in [GPS13] that the measure τ\tau defines a parametrization of γ\gamma. Some of the challenges in proving this are discussed in [GPS13, Sections 1.2 and 5.3].

As a first step towards proving Theorem 1.4, we prove the following in Section 3.

Theorem 1.6.

In Theorem 1.4, one can choose clc_{\operatorname{l}} in (4) such that τ=𝔪γ\tau=\mathfrak{m}_{\gamma} a.s.

We end this subsection by commenting on our proof ideas for Theorems 1.6 and 1.4. On the one hand, the proof of Theorem 1.6 closely follows [GPS13, Section 4] with the simplification that we work directly in the continuum, hence our one-point and two-point estimates are power laws with no sub-polynomial corrections, in contrast to the arm exponent estimates for percolation. On the other hand, an additional technicality arises when we try to implement the continuum analog of a strong coupling result from [GPS13, Section 4]. See the beginning of Section 3 for more discussion. Our proof of Theorem 1.9 below uses the same idea as in Theorem 1.6. However, Theorem 1.6 itself is not sufficient for proving Theorem 1.4 due to the presence of double points in SLE6\SLE_{6}. To deal with this issue, we prove that the occupation measure of the frontier of SLE6\SLE_{6} is 0 and use it to conclude the proof of Theorem 1.4 in Section 5.

1.2 The natural measure on pivotal points

Let Ω\Omega be a Jordan domain with smooth boundary and sample ωη\omega_{\eta} from Ber⁡(Ωη)\operatorname{Ber}(\Omega_{\eta}). Let a,b,c,d∈∂Ωa,b,c,d\in{\partial}\Omega be four distinct points ordered counterclockwise. For η\eta small enough such that aηa_{\eta}, bηb_{\eta}, cηc_{\eta}, and dηd_{\eta} are distinct. the following three sentences describe the same event.

    There is a path {vi}1≤i≤n\{v_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq n} such that v1v_{1} and vnv_{n} are on Δbη,cη​Ωη\Delta_{b_{\eta},c_{\eta}}\Omega_{\eta} and Δdη,aη​Ωη\Delta_{d_{\eta},a_{\eta}}\Omega_{\eta} respectively, while viv_{i} is a white inner vertex for all 1<i<n1<i<n.

  • •

    Let e¯η\overline{e}_{\eta} be the first edge crossed by the percolation interface on (Ωη,cη,aη)(\Omega_{\eta},c_{\eta},a_{\eta}) with one endpoint lying on Δdη,bη​Ωη\Delta_{d_{\eta},b_{\eta}}\Omega_{\eta}. Then e¯η\overline{e}_{\eta} has an endpoint on Δdη,aη​Ωη\Delta_{d_{\eta},a_{\eta}}\Omega_{\eta}.

Denote this event by EηE_{\eta}. Consider the pair of curves (γη1,γη2)(\gamma^{1}_{\eta},\gamma^{2}_{\eta}) defined as follows. When EηE_{\eta} occurs, let γη1\gamma^{1}_{\eta} and γη2\gamma^{2}_{\eta} be the percolation interfaces on (Ω,aη,bη)(\Omega,a_{\eta},b_{\eta}) and (Ωη,cη,dη)(\Omega_{\eta},c_{\eta},d_{\eta}), respectively. Otherwise, let γη1\gamma^{1}_{\eta} and γη2\gamma^{2}_{\eta} be the percolation interfaces on (Ω,aη,dη)(\Omega,a_{\eta},d_{\eta}) and (Ωη,cη,bη)(\Omega_{\eta},c_{\eta},b_{\eta}), respectively. Given an event defined in terms of ωη\omega_{\eta}, a site in Ωη\Omega_{\eta} is called a pivotal point for this event if flipping the color of the site changes the outcome of the event. Let 𝒫η\mathcal{P}_{\eta} be the set of pivotal points for EηE_{\eta}. Then a site of Ωη\Omega_{\eta} belongs to 𝒫η\mathcal{P}_{\eta} if and only if it is the endpoint of one edge crossed by γη1\gamma^{1}_{\eta} and one edge crossed by γη2\gamma^{2}_{\eta}.

The picture above has a natural scaling limit. Let ∂a,bΩ{\partial}_{a,b}\Omega be the counterclockwise arc on ∂Ω{\partial}\Omega between aa and bb. By locality, we can couple the chordal SLE6\SLE_{6} on (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b) to the chordal SLE6 on (Ω,a,d)(\Omega,a,d) such that the two curves agree until hitting the arc ∂b,dΩ{\partial}_{b,d}\Omega, after which they evolve independently. Let EE be the event that the hitting location on ∂b,dΩ{\partial}_{b,d}\Omega lies on ∂b,cΩ{\partial}_{b,c}\Omega. If EE occurs (resp., does not occur), let γ1\gamma^{1} be the SLE6\SLE_{6} from aa to bb (resp., dd) so that there exists a unique connected component of Ω∖γ1\Omega\setminus\gamma^{1} whose boundary contains cc and dd (resp. bb). Conditioning on γ1\gamma^{1}, let γ2\gamma^{2} be a chordal SLE6\SLE_{6} on this component from cc to dd (resp. bb).

A point is called a pivotal point for EE if and only if it is on the range of both γ1\gamma^{1} and γ2\gamma^{2}. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the set of pivotal points of EE. Fix cp>0c_{\operatorname{p}}>0 and define

μη:=cp​∑z∈𝒫ηδz​η2α4η​(η,1),\mu_{\eta}:=c_{\operatorname{p}}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{P}_{\eta}}\delta_{z}\frac{\eta^{2}}{\alpha^{\eta}_{4}(\eta,1)}, (5)

where α4η​(η,1)\alpha^{\eta}_{4}(\eta,1) is a normalizing constant which will be specified in Section 2.4.

The following theorem follows from [GPS13].

Theorem 1.7.

There is a coupling of (γη1,γη2)(\gamma^{1}_{\eta},\gamma^{2}_{\eta}) and (γ1,γ2)(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}) such that a.s.,

  • (1)

    𝟏𝔼η\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{E}_{\eta}} converges to 𝟏E\mathbf{1}_{E},

  • (2)

    (γη1,γη2)(\gamma^{1}_{\eta},\gamma^{2}_{\eta}) converges to (γ1,γ2)(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}) in the d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}}-metric, and

  • (3)

Certain basic properties of μ\mu were also proved in [GPS13], for example that μ\mu is measurable with respect to the scaling limit of percolation in quad-crossing space (see Section 2 for definitions) and the conformal covariance of μ\mu.

As we will explain in more detail in Section 4, (see the discussion above Lemmas 4.1 and 4.3) the set 𝒫\mathcal{P} is locally absolutely continuous with respect to the set of cut points of two-dimensional Brownian motion, whose occupation measure is the subject of [HLLS18]. Using the relationship between 𝒫\mathcal{P} and Brownian cut points we will prove the following result in Section 4.

Proposition 1.8.

The occupation measure 𝔪𝒫\mathfrak{m}_{\mathcal{P}} of 𝒫\mathcal{P} a.s. exists and is defined by its 3/43/4-dimensional Minkowski content in the sense of Definition 1.2.

In Section 4, we use the same arguments as for Theorem 1.6 to conclude the following.

Theorem 1.9.

In Theorem 1.7, one can choose cpc_{\operatorname{p}} in (5) such that μ=𝔪𝒫\mu=\mathfrak{m}_{\mathcal{P}} a.s.

Theorem 1.9 confirms that the scaling limit of the pivotal measure in [GPS13] is in fact induced by the 3/43/4-dimensional Minkowski content of the continuum pivotal points. We can also consider double points of SLE6\SLE_{6} and the points of intersection of CLE6\CLE_{6} loops, which describe the full scaling limit of the interfaces between black and white clusters in critical percolation [CN06]. In these cases, the analog of Theorem 1.9 holds since their local pictures are absolutely continuous with respect to each other and the Minkowski content is defined locally. We restrict to the formulation in Theorem 1.9 for concreteness.

Theorem 1.9 is an important ingredient of the first and third authors’ proof [HS19] of the convergence of uniform triangulations to Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) with parameter 8/3\sqrt{8/3} under the so-called Cardy embedding, which is a discrete conformal embedding based on percolation. A key tool in the proof is the Liouville dynamical percolation (LDP) introduced in [GHSS19], which is a variant of the ordinary dynamical percolation considered in [GPS18]. The discrete (ordinary) dynamical percolation in [GPS18] is defined as follows. We start from a sample of critical Bernoulli site percolation and then use i.i.d. exponential clocks at each site to update the color. The discrete LDP is defined in the same way except that the rates of the exponential clocks are not identical but depend on a background LQG surface. The continuous LDP is the continuum limit of the discrete LDP as the lattice size and the clock rates are rescaled appropriately. By the existence of the scaling limit of the pivotal measure from [GPS13], the existence of the continuous LDP was proved in [GHSS19] in the so-called quad-crossing topology (see Section 2.2), similarly as in [GPS18].

The key idea of [HS19] is to consider ordinary dynamical percolation (namely, with i.i.d. clocks) on a uniform triangulation and realize that under the conformal embedding the scaling limit of this dynamic is the continuous LDP. Once this is proved, ergodicity of continuous LDP proved in [GHSS19] implies that uniform triangulations under the Cardy embedding converge to LQG. The quad-crossing topology allows [GHSS19] to apply the powerful machinery of noise sensitivity developed in [GPS10] to prove the desired ergodicity of continuous LDP. However, it is not the natural topology to describe the scaling limit of the ordinary dynamical percolation on uniform triangulations. The natural topology is given by the mating-of-trees framework of Duplantier, Miller, and Sheffield [DMS14]; also see [GHS19].

The technical bulk of [HS19] is to show that the quad-crossing and mating-of-trees descriptions of continuous LDP are equivalent. In both descriptions, the dynamic is determined by its initial configuration and a Poisson point process whose intensity measure is supported on the set of pivotal points, and the equivalence of the LDP descriptions can therefore be reduced to the equivalence of two notions of pivotal measure. The notion of pivotal measure coming from [GHSS19] is given by the ordinary pivotal measure in [GPS13] weighted by the exponential of a Gaussian free field. The notion coming from mating-of-trees, which is introduced in [BHS18], is defined using Brownian motion and involves neither the ordinary pivotal measure from [GPS13] nor Gaussian free field. To show the equivalence of these two notions of pivotal measure, the description of ordinary pivotal measure in terms of Minkowski content as in Theorem 1.9 plays an important role. In particular, with this definition the equivalence of the two pivotal measures becomes a natural and concrete statement for CLE6\CLE_{6}. See [HS19, Section 5] for the detail of this argument and see [HS19, Section 1.4] for an overview of the entire program.

2 Preliminaries

In this section we review some basic facts about percolation which are used in later proofs. Most facts are either known or easy consequences of known results. Therefore we will be brief and refer to [SW01, SS11, GPS13, Wer09] for more details.

2.1 Basic notations

Throughout the paper, we use γ\gamma and γη\gamma_{\eta} to represent SLE6\SLE_{6} and the percolation interface, respectively. Both γ\gamma and γη\gamma_{\eta} are understood as continuous curves modulo reparametrization unless otherwise specified. When there is no risk of confusion, we also use γ,γη\gamma,\gamma_{\eta} to denote the range of the curves.

For all R>0R>0 and z∈ℂ=ℝ2z\in\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}^{2}, we let ℬR​(z)=z+[−R,R]2\mathcal{B}_{R}(z)=z+[-R,R]^{2} denote the square of side length 2​R2R centered at zz. We call a set a box if it can be written on this form. We write ℬR\mathcal{B}_{R} for ℬR​(0)\mathcal{B}_{R}(0) and c​ℬR​(z)c\mathcal{B}_{R}(z) for z+[−R​c,R​c]2z+[-Rc,Rc]^{2} (instead of c​z+[−R​c,R​c]2cz+[-Rc,Rc]^{2}) for all c>0c>0. For 0<r<R0<r<R, let A⁡(r,R)=ℬR∖ℬrA(r,R)=\mathcal{B}_{R}\setminus{\mathcal{B}_{r}}. We call a domain AA an annulus if AA is topologically equivalent to A⁡(1,2)A(1,2), and we use ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A to denote its inner and outer boundaries, respectively.

Given any two sets X,Y⊂ℝ2X,Y\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, we write dist(X,Y):=inf{|x−y|:x∈X,y∈Y}\mathrm{dist}(X,Y):=\inf\{|x-y|:x\in X,\,y\in Y\}. Let X¯\overline{X} denote the closure of XX. If X¯⊂Y\overline{X}\subset Y, we write X⋐YX\Subset Y.

We use classical asymptotic notations. Given two non-negative functions ff and gg, we write f≲gf\lesssim g (resp., f≳gf\gtrsim g) if there is a constant C>0C>0 such that f⁡(x)≤C​g​(x)f(x)\leq Cg(x) (resp., f⁡(x)≥C​g​(x)f(x)\geq Cg(x)) for all xx. We also write f=O⁡(g)f=O(g) when f≲gf\lesssim g. We write f≍gf\asymp g if f≲gf\lesssim g and g≲fg\lesssim f. We say f​(x)=ox​(1)f(x)=o_{x}(1) as x→ax\to a if limx→af⁡(x)=0\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=0.

2.2 Quad-crossing representations of percolation

There are various ways to represent the scaling limit of critical planar percolation (see e.g. the introduction of [SS11]). One way is to use its crossing information, as we review now.

A quad in ℂ\mathbb{C} is a homeomorphism Q:[0,1]2→ℂQ:[0,1]^{2}\to\mathbb{C}. Let

∂1Q:=Q⁡({0}×[0,1]),∂2Q:=Q⁡([0,1]×{0}),\displaystyle\partial_{1}Q:=Q(\{0\}\times[0,1]),\quad\partial_{2}Q:=Q([0,1]\times\{0\}),
∂3Q:=Q⁡({1}×[0,1]),∂4Q:=Q⁡([0,1]×{1}).\displaystyle\partial_{3}Q:=Q(\{1\}\times[0,1]),\quad\partial_{4}Q:=Q([0,1]\times\{1\}).

We will identify a quad QQ with (Q​[0,1]2,Q⁡(0,0),Q⁡(1,0),Q⁡(1,1),(0,1))(Q[0,1]^{2},Q(0,0),Q(1,0),Q(1,1),(0,1)), so quads giving the same such tuple are identified. Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be the space of quads in ℂ\mathbb{C}, equipped with the uniform topology. A crossing of a quad QQ is a closed set in ℂ\mathbb{C} containing a connected closed subset of Q⁡([0,1]2)Q([0,1]^{2}) that intersects both ∂1Q\partial_{1}Q and ∂3Q\partial_{3}Q. Given Q1,Q2Q_{1},Q_{2} in ℂ\mathbb{C}, we say Q1≤Q2Q_{1}\leq Q_{2} if every crossing of Q2Q_{2} contains a crossing of Q1Q_{1}. We say Q1<Q2Q_{1}<Q_{2} if there exists a neighborhood of 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) of QiQ_{i} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} such that N1≤N2N_{1}\leq N_{2} for any Ni∈𝒩iN_{i}\in\mathcal{N}_{i}. A quad-crossing configuration on ℂ\mathbb{C} is a function ω:𝒬→{0,1}\omega:\mathcal{Q}\to\{0,1\} such that the set ω−1​(1)\omega^{-1}(1) is closed in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and for any Q1,Q2Q_{1},Q_{2} with Q1<Q2Q_{1}<Q_{2}, we have ω⁡(Q2)≤ω⁡(Q1)\omega(Q_{2})\leq\omega(Q_{1}). We denote the space of quad-crossing configurations on ℂ\mathbb{C} by ℋ\mathcal{H}. The set ℋ\mathcal{H} can be endowed with a metric dℋd_{\mathcal{H}} such that (ℋ,dℋ)(\mathcal{H},d_{\mathcal{H}}) is compact and separable.

Let Ω⫋ℂ\Omega\subsetneqq\mathbb{C} be an open set and let 𝒬Ω\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega} be the space of quads with image in Ω\Omega. By restricting to 𝒬Ω\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega}, each element in ℋ\mathcal{H} induces a quad-crossing configuration on Ω\Omega. Let ℋΩ\mathcal{H}_{\Omega} be the space of such configurations, endowed with the metric induced by dℋd_{\mathcal{H}}, which we still denote by dℋd_{\mathcal{H}}. We refer to [SS11, GPS13] for more details on (ℋΩ,dℋ)(\mathcal{H}_{\Omega},d_{\mathcal{H}}). Here we only record the following facts. Suppose Ω\Omega is a Jordan domain and that ωη\omega_{\eta} is sampled from Ber⁡(Ωη)\operatorname{Ber}(\Omega_{\eta}). We identify ωη\omega_{\eta} with an element in ℋΩ\mathcal{H}_{\Omega} by setting ωη​(Q)=1\omega_{\eta}(Q)=1 if and only if the white sites of ωη\omega_{\eta} form a crossing of QQ. Then ωη\omega_{\eta} weakly converges to a random variable ω\omega in ℋΩ\mathcal{H}_{\Omega} under the dℋd_{\mathcal{H}}-metric. Moreover,

  1. 1.

    for each deterministic quad Q∈𝒬ΩQ\in\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega}, in any coupling where ωη→ω\omega_{\eta}\to\omega a.s., we have ωη​(Q)→ω​(Q)\omega_{\eta}(Q)\to\omega(Q) in probability;

  2. 2.

    there exists a countable collection {Qn}n∈ℕ⊂𝒬Ω\{Q_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega} such that QnQ_{n} has piecewise smooth boundary and {ω⁡(Qn)}n∈ℕ\{\omega(Q_{n})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} generates the Borel σ\sigma-field of (ℋΩ,dℋ)(\mathcal{H}_{\Omega},d_{\mathcal{H}}).

2.3 Some scaling limit results

The following scaling limit result is from [CN06] and [GPS13].

Theorem 2.1.

Suppose Ω\Omega is a Jordan domain. Sample ωη\omega_{\eta} from Ber⁡(Ωη)\operatorname{Ber}(\Omega_{\eta}). Then there is a coupling of (ωη)η>0(\omega_{\eta})_{\eta>0} such that the following hold.

  1. 1.

    For any fixed x,y∈∂Ωx,y\in\partial\Omega with x≠yx\neq y, the interface γηx​y\gamma^{xy}_{\eta} on (Ωη,xη,yη)(\Omega_{\eta},x_{\eta},y_{\eta}) converges in probability to an SLE6\SLE_{6} curve γx​y\gamma^{xy} on (Ω,x,y)(\Omega,x,y) under the d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}}-metric.

  2. 2.

    The quad-crossing configuration ωη\omega_{\eta} converges to ω\omega in probability under the dℋd_{\mathcal{H}}-metric.

In particular, this provides a coupling of ω\omega and {γx​y:x≠y,x,y∈∂Ω}\{\gamma^{xy}:x\neq y,\;x,y\in{\partial}\Omega\}.

Theorem 2.1 is obtained by considering the collection of disjoint loops Γη\Gamma_{\eta} which are interfaces between black and white clusters of ωη\omega_{\eta}. They converge to a random collection of loops Γ\Gamma called the conformal loop ensemble with κ=6\kappa=6 (CLE6) on Ω\Omega. Moreover, both {γx​y}x,y∈∂Ω\{\gamma^{xy}\}_{x,y\in{\partial}\Omega} and ω\omega are measurable with respect to the CLE6\CLE_{6} (see [CN06] and [GPS13, Section 2.3]). We will not give more detail on CLE6\CLE_{6} as it is not needed, but refer to [CN06, She09] for further details.

We have seen several classes of domains so far. For the definition of SLE6\SLE_{6}, we assumed that the boundary is a continuous image of a circle. For quad-crossing space, we considered general domains. For Theorem 2.1, we considered Jordan domains. In Theorems 1.4 and 1.9, we assumed that ∂Ω{\partial}\Omega is a smooth Jordan curve. We will carefully organize the argument so that Theorem 2.1 does not have to be extended to domains with rougher boundary. See Remark 3.7.

The following gives the convergence of the interface at the hitting time of certain domains. The lemma will be used to prove Lemmas 2.9, 2.10, and 5.1.

Lemma 2.2.

In the setting of Theorem 1.4, view γ,γη:[0,1]→Ω\gamma,\gamma_{\eta}:[0,1]\to\Omega as parametrized curves coupled together such that limη→0sup0≤t≤1{|γη​(t)−γ⁡(t)|}=0\lim_{\eta\to 0}\sup_{0\leq t\leq 1}\{|\gamma_{\eta}(t)-\gamma(t)|\}=0 a.s. (The existence of such parametrizations and couplings is guaranteed by d𝒰d_{\mathcal{U}}-convergence of γη\gamma_{\eta} to γ\gamma.) Let ση,σ\sigma_{\eta},\sigma be stopping times for γη\gamma_{\eta} and γ\gamma, respectively, such that ση→σ\sigma_{\eta}\to\sigma a.s. Fix a piecewise smooth simple curve ℓ⋐Ω\ell\Subset\Omega such that ℙ[γ(σ)∈ℓ]=0\mathbb{P}[\gamma(\sigma)\in\ell]=0. Let λ=inf{t≥σ:γ⁡(t)∈ℓ}\lambda=\inf\{t\geq\sigma:\gamma(t)\in\ell\} and λη=inf{t≥ση:γη​(t)∈ℓ}\lambda_{\eta}=\inf\{t\geq\sigma_{\eta}:\gamma_{\eta}(t)\in\ell\}. Then λη→λ\lambda_{\eta}\to\lambda a.s.

Proof.

With probability 11, there exist sequences of rational times tη↓λt_{\eta}\downarrow\lambda and sη↑λs_{\eta}\uparrow\lambda for η→0\eta\to 0 in a countable set such that γ⁡([sη,tη])∩ℓ≠∅\gamma([s_{\eta},t_{\eta}])\cap\ell\neq\emptyset. This can be easily proved by way of contradiction, by using that an SLE6 curve will a.s. cross a deterministic smooth curve upon hitting it. Now the lemma follows from the continuity of γ\gamma. ∎

2.4 Arm events

Given a percolation configuration ωη\omega_{\eta} and an annulus AA, we say that an alternating 4-arm event occurs for AA if and only if there are four disjoint monochromatic paths connecting ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A such that the color sequence of the four paths is alternating between black and white. There is an ambiguity in the definition due to the lattice effect at the boundary. However the precise convention does not matter as η→0\eta\to 0 so we ignore it. In the continuum, suppose AA is an annulus such that ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A are piecewise smooth. For A⋐ΩA\Subset\Omega, a quad-crossing configuration ω∈ℋΩ\omega\in\mathcal{H}_{\Omega} is said to belong to the alternating 4-arm event of AA if there exist quads Qi⊂𝒬ΩQ_{i}\subset\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega}, i=1,2,3,4i=1,2,3,4, with the following properties:

  • (i)

    Q1Q_{1} and Q3Q_{3} are disjoint and at positive distance from each other, and the same hold for Q2Q_{2} and Q4Q_{4}.

  • (ii)

    For i∈{1,3}i\in\{1,3\}, the side ∂1Qi{\partial}_{1}Q_{i} lies inside ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and the side ∂3Qi{\partial}_{3}Q_{i} lies outside ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A; for i∈{2,4}i\in\{2,4\}, the side ∂2Qi{\partial}_{2}Q_{i} lies inside ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and the side ∂4Qi{\partial}_{4}Q_{i} lies outside ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A; all these sides are of positive distance away from AA and from the other QjQ_{j}’s.

  • (iii)

    The four quads are ordered cyclically around AA according to their indices.

  • (iv)

    ω⁡(Q1)=ω⁡(Q3)=1\omega(Q_{1})=\omega(Q_{3})=1 and ω⁡(Q2)=ω⁡(Q4)=0\omega(Q_{2})=\omega(Q_{4})=0.

In both the discrete and the continuum, the general kk-arm event in AA given any prescribed color pattern can be defined similarly. For ωη\omega_{\eta} coming from a percolation configuration, the two definitions of arm events agree.

Convention 2.3.

In the rest of the paper, for each k=2,3,4,5k=2,3,4,5, we focus on arm events with particular color conditions. For k=4k=4, it is the alternating 4-arm event. For k=2,3,5k=2,3,5, it is the kk-arm event where not all arms have the same color. We will call these events the kk-arm event without mentioning the color pattern. We will not need the case k≠2,3,4,5k\neq 2,3,4,5.

Now we are ready to describe the normalizing constants in (4) and (5).

Remark 2.4 (Normalizing constants).

We use αkη​(η,1)\alpha^{\eta}_{k}(\eta,1) (k=2,4k=2,4) to denote the probability of the kk-arm event (under Convention 2.3) from the single site at the origin to ∂ℬ1\partial\mathcal{B}_{1}. Then α2η​(η,1)\alpha^{\eta}_{2}(\eta,1) and α4η​(η,1)\alpha^{\eta}_{4}(\eta,1) are the normalizing constants in (4) and (5), respectively. It is known that αkη​(η,1)=η(k2−1)/12+oη​(1)\alpha^{\eta}_{k}(\eta,1)=\eta^{(k^{2}-1)/12+o_{\eta}(1)} [SW01]. The up-to-constant asymptotics are open.

In the coupling of Theorem 2.1, for k=2,3,4,5k=2,3,4,5, let 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} be kk-arm events for an annulus A⊂ΩA\subset\Omega as in Convention 2.3. Then the event 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} is a.s. measurable with respect to the Borel σ\sigma-algebra of (ℋΩ,dℋ)(\mathcal{H}_{\Omega},d_{\mathcal{H}}) [GPS13, Section 2]. As explained in [SW01], the events 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} can be expressed in terms of percolation exploration to give

limη→0ℙ[ωη∈𝒜k]=ℙ[ω∈𝒜k]for k=2,3,4,5.\lim_{\eta\to 0}\mathbb{P}[\omega_{\eta}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}]=\mathbb{P}[\omega\in\mathcal{A}_{k}]\qquad\textrm{for }k=2,3,4,5. (6)

Lemma 2.9 in [GPS13] gives the following stronger version of (6) when k=2,3,4k=2,3,4. (This is expected to be true also for k=5k=5, but this is not proved in [GPS13] and is not needed.)

Lemma 2.5.

limη→0ℙ[{ω∈𝒜k}△{ωη∈𝒜k}]=0\lim_{\eta\to 0}\mathbb{P}[\{\omega\in\mathcal{A}_{k}\}\mathbin{\triangle}\{\omega_{\eta}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}\}]=0 for k=2,3,4k=2,3,4.

For R>r>0R>r>0 and A=A⁡(r,R)A=A(r,R) write αk(r,R)=ℙ[ω∈𝒜k]\alpha_{k}(r,R)=\mathbb{P}[\omega\in\mathcal{A}_{k}]. The up-to-constant asymptotic for αk​(r,R)\alpha_{k}(r,R) is well-known [SW01, Equation (14)] (c.f. Remark 2.4):

αk(r,R)≍(r/R)(k2−1)/12,for k=2,3,4,5.\displaystyle\alpha_{k}(r,R)\asymp(r/R)^{(k^{2}-1)/12},\quad\textrm{for }k=2,3,4,5. (7)

An important property of ω\omega as an element in ℋ\mathcal{H} is the monotonicity built in its definition. The following monotonicity results will be used repeatedly.

Lemma 2.6.

In the coupling of Theorem 2.1, let γ:=γa​b\gamma:=\gamma^{ab} and γη:=γηa​b\gamma_{\eta}:=\gamma^{ab}_{\eta} for two given distinct points a,b∈∂Ωa,b\in\partial\Omega. View (γη,γ)(\gamma_{\eta},\gamma) as parametrized curves as in Lemma 2.2. For each fixed t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), let KtK_{t} be the hull of γ⁡([0,t])\gamma([0,t]). Namely, KtK_{t} is the complement of the connected component of Ω∖γ⁡([0,t])\Omega\setminus\gamma([0,t]) containing the target of γ\gamma. For any annulus A⋐ΩA\Subset\Omega, let A1A_{1} be the inside of ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and A2A_{2} be the outside of ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A. Then for the quad-crossing configuration ω\omega,

  1. 1.

    if ∂1A∩γ≠∅{\partial}_{1}A\cap\gamma\neq\emptyset, then the 2-arm event for AA occurs a.s., and

  2. 2.

    if there exists t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] such that ∂Kt∩A1≠∅{\partial}K_{t}\cap A_{1}\neq\emptyset and γ⁡(t)∈A2\gamma(t)\in A_{2}, then the 3-arm event for AA occurs a.s.

Proof.

For Assertion 1, choose t,δ∈(0,1)t,\delta\in(0,1) such that γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) is inside ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A and dist⁡(γ⁡(t),∂1A)>δ\mathrm{dist}(\gamma(t),{\partial}_{1}A)>\delta. Since limη→0sup0≤t≤1{|γη​(t)−γ⁡(t)|}=0\lim_{\eta\to 0}\sup_{0\leq t\leq 1}\{|\gamma_{\eta}(t)-\gamma(t)|\}=0 a.s., we have dist⁡(γη​(t),∂1A)>0.5​δ\mathrm{dist}(\gamma_{\eta}(t),{\partial}_{1}A)>0.5\delta for small enough η\eta. In this case the 2-arm event for AA occurs for ωη\omega_{\eta}. Sending η→0\eta\to 0 and applying Lemma 2.5, we get Assertion 1.

Assertion 2 can be proved similarly. See Figure 1. Since γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) is a boundary point of KtK_{t}, there exists a δ>0\delta>0 and a path ρ\rho starting from some point in A1A_{1} and ending at some point in A2A_{2} such that dist⁡(ρ,γ⁡([0,t]))>δ\mathrm{dist}(\rho,\gamma([0,t]))>\delta. Without loss of generality assume the set ∂Kt∩A1\partial K_{t}\cap A_{1} contains a point on left frontier of γ⁡([0,t])\gamma([0,t]). Now for small enough η\eta, we have dist⁡(ρ,γη​([0,t]))>0.5​δ\mathrm{dist}(\rho,\gamma_{\eta}([0,t]))>0.5\delta. On the other hand, by the argument for Assertion 1, for η\eta small enough the there exists a black arm β\beta of ωη\omega_{\eta} from ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A to ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A. In this case, there must be a white arm of ωη\omega_{\eta} on each connected component of A∖(ρ∪β)A\setminus(\rho\cup\beta) from ∂1A{\partial}_{1}A to ∂2A{\partial}_{2}A, hence the 3-arm event for AA occurs for ωη\omega_{\eta}. Now Assertion 2 follows from Lemma 2.5. ∎

The following variant of Lemma 2.6 can be proved similarly. We omit the details.

Lemma 2.7.

Consider a coupling where both the conditions in Theorems 1.7 and 2.1 are satisfied so that (ω,γ1,γ2)(\omega,\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}) are coupled. Let A,A1,A2A,A_{1},A_{2} be defined as in Lemma 2.6. Then on the event 𝒫∩A1≠∅\mathcal{P}\cap A_{1}\neq\emptyset, the 4-arm event for AA occurs a.s. for ω\omega.

The event γ∩A1≠∅\gamma\cap A_{1}\neq\emptyset in Lemma 2.6 is simply the 2-arm event with the further requirement that each of the two boundary arcs contain one endpoint of the arm. The similar statement holds for 𝒫∩A1≠∅\mathcal{P}\cap A_{1}\neq\emptyset in Lemma 2.7. By the following lemma, these endpoint requirements only decrease the probability by a constant factor.

Lemma 2.8.

In the setting of Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7, let ℬ⊂Ω\mathcal{B}\subset\Omega be a box of radius ε\varepsilon whose center is r>10​εr>10\varepsilon away from ∂Ω{\partial}\Omega. Then ℙ[γ∩ℬ≠∅]≍α2(ε,r)\mathbb{P}[\gamma\cap\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset]\asymp\alpha_{2}(\varepsilon,r) and ℙ[𝒫∩ℬ≠∅]≍α4(ε,r)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{P}\cap\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset]\asymp\alpha_{4}(\varepsilon,r), where the implicit constants in ≍\asymp only depend on Ω\Omega but not on other parameters.

Proof.

The 2-arm case follows from the classical one-point estimate of SLE6\SLE_{6}. See e.g. [LR15]. The 4-arm case follows from [GPS13, Proposition 4.9]. ∎

2.5 Face induced by the percolation exploration

Given a box ℬ\mathcal{B} and two distinct points x1,x2∈∂ℬx_{1},x_{2}\in{\partial}\mathcal{B}, let θ1\theta_{1} (resp., θ2\theta_{2}) be a simple path joining x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} (resp., x2x_{2} and x1x_{1}). If the pair of paths Θ={θ1,θ2}\Theta=\{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\} is such that there exists a domain 𝒟Θ\mathcal{D}_{\Theta} with ℬ⊂𝒟Θ\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\Theta} and ∂𝒟Θ=θ1∪θ2{\partial}\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}=\theta_{1}\cup\theta_{2}, then we call Θ\Theta a face at ℬ\mathcal{B} with endpoints x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}.

Let Ω\Omega be a simply connected domain whose boundary is a continuous curve and let a,b∈∂Ωa,b\in{\partial}\Omega be such that a≠ba\neq b. Suppose γ\gamma is a SLE6 on (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b) parametrized in an arbitrary way and ℬ⊂Ω\mathcal{B}\subset\Omega is a box. Throughout this subsection we write (Ω,a,b)(\Omega,a,b) as Ω\Omega whenever it simplifies the notation and cause no confusion. For example, we use 𝒜⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{B},\Omega) to denote the event {γ∩ℬ≠∅}\{\gamma\cap\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset\} although this event depends on a,ba,b. On 𝒜⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{B},\Omega), let

σ¯=inf{t:γt∈ℬ},\displaystyle\underaccent{\bar}{\sigma}=\inf\{t:\gamma_{t}\in\mathcal{B}\},\quad σ¯=sup{t:γt∈ℬ},\displaystyle\overline{\sigma}=\sup\{t:\gamma_{t}\in\mathcal{B}\},
x1=γ⁡(σ¯),\displaystyle x_{1}=\gamma(\underaccent{\bar}{\sigma}), x2=γ⁡(σ¯).\displaystyle x_{2}=\gamma(\overline{\sigma}).

Let 𝒟⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B},\Omega) be the connected component of Ω∖(γ[0,σ¯]∪γ[σ¯,∞))\Omega\setminus(\gamma[0,\underaccent{\bar}{\sigma}]\cup\gamma[\overline{\sigma},\infty)) containing ℬ\mathcal{B}. Then 𝒟⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B},\Omega) can be viewed as a (random) face at ℬ\mathcal{B} with the arcs ∂x1,x2𝒟⁡(ℬ,Ω){\partial}_{x_{1},x_{2}}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B},\Omega) and ∂x2,x1𝒟⁡(ℬ,Ω){\partial}_{x_{2},x_{1}}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B},\Omega), which we call the face at ℬ\mathcal{B} induced by γ\gamma. Lemma 2.9.

Lemma 2.10.

In the setting of Lemma 2.9, let 𝒜3\mathcal{A}_{3} represent the 33-arm event for U∖ℬU\setminus\mathcal{B}. Then ℙ[𝒜(ℬ,Ω)∖𝒢Ω(ℬ,U)]≤ℙ[ω∈𝒜3].\mathbb{P}\left[{\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{B},\Omega)\setminus\mathcal{G}_{\Omega}(\mathcal{B},U)}\right]\leq\mathbb{P}[{\omega\in\mathcal{A}_{3}}].

In the setting of Theorem 2.1, it is clear that ω\omega inherits the spatial independence property from ωη\omega_{\eta}. By Lemma 2.9, we get the following.

Lemma 2.11.

In the setting of Lemma 2.9, let Ω1,Ω2\Omega_{1},\Omega_{2} be two disjoint open subsets in Ω\Omega. Then ω\omega restricted to 𝒬Ω1\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega_{1}} and to 𝒬Ω2\mathcal{Q}_{\Omega_{2}} are independent as random variables in ℋΩ1\mathcal{H}_{\Omega_{1}} and ℋΩ2\mathcal{H}_{\Omega_{2}}, respectively. Moreover, ω\omega restricted to 𝒬ℬ\mathcal{Q}_{\mathcal{B}} is independent of 𝒟⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B},\Omega).

3 Equivalence of the two measures on the interface

This section is devoted to proving Theorem 1.6 hence we retain the notations in the statement of the theorem. To prove Theorem 1.6, we use the L2L^{2} framework as in [GPS13], which is based on a strong coupling scheme and the spatial independence of percolation. Since we work in the continuum, some issues in [GPS13, Section 4] can be simplified. In particular, the required one-point and two-point estimates that we will rely on are are power laws with no sub-polynomial corrections (see Lemmas 3.3—3.5), while a major novelty of [GPS13, Section 4] is obtaining scaling limit results despite the unknown sub-polynomial corrections in the percolation estimates. After we prepare the one-point and two-point estimates, we reduce Theorem 1.6 to a strong coupling estimate (21). This reduction is a straightforward adaptation of the L2L^{2} argument in [GPS13, Section 4], nevertheless we still include the full argument for completeness and hence follow closely both the method and the presentation in [GPS13, Section 4]. To prove the strong coupling estimate (21), we would like to apply its discrete analog from [GPS13] and then pass to the continuum. However, a straightforward implementation of this idea only gives Lemma 3.6, a weaker variant of (21). The reason is that when we pass from percolation to its continuum limit, we rely on Theorem 2.1, which is for Jordan domains. On the other hand, the domain boundary considered in (21) is the exterior boundary of SLE6\SLE_{6}, which is not simple. Instead of trying to strengthen the convergence in Theorem 2.1 to include certain non-Jordan domains, we will use an argument directly in the continuum to go from Lemma 3.6 to the desired (21). We now carry out the plan above in detail.

Let ℬ⋐Ω\mathcal{B}\Subset\Omega be a box whose four vertices are on ∪k∈ℕ2−kℤ2\cup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}2^{-k}\mathbb{Z}^{2}. Let ε∈{2−k:k∈ℕ}\varepsilon\in\{2^{-k}:k\in\mathbb{N}\}. Assume ε\varepsilon is small enough such that ε<dist⁡(ℬ,∂Ω)\varepsilon<\mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{B},{\partial}\Omega). Yε=#⁡{1≤i≤p:γ∩2​Qi≠∅}.Y^{\varepsilon}=\#\{1\leq i\leq p:\gamma\cap 2Q_{i}\neq\emptyset\}.

Remark 3.7.

We assume that Ω′\Omega^{\prime} is a Jordan domain in Lemma 3.6 because our proof crucially relies on the coupling result of [GPS13] in the discrete and the convergence result Theorem 2.1, which is only established for Jordan domains [CN06]. Lemma 3.6 is not directly applicable to 𝒟i,𝒟j\mathcal{D}_{i},\mathcal{D}_{j} in (21) since they are a.s. not Jordan (see Figure 1). To overcome this issue, we extend Lemma 3.6 to Lemma 3.8 below.

Lemma 3.8.

Suppose Ω′\Omega^{\prime} is a simply connected domain containing the origin whose boundary is a continuous curve. Let ϕ:I→ℂ\phi:I\to\mathbb{C} be a parametrization of ∂Ω′\partial\Omega^{\prime} for I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} an interval, and let

dbl={z∈∂Ω′:∃s≠t​such  that ​ϕ​(s)=ϕ⁡(t)=z}.\mathrm{dbl}=\{z\in{\partial}\Omega^{\prime}:\exists s\neq t\;\textrm{such\,\,that\,}\;\phi(s)=\phi(t)=z\}.

Suppose dist⁡(γ′,dbl)>0\mathrm{dist}(\gamma^{\prime},\mathrm{dbl})>0 a.s. Then ℙ[dist(ϕ−1(γ′),ϕ−1(dbl))<δ]=oδ(1)\mathbb{P}[\mathrm{dist}(\phi^{-1}(\gamma^{\prime}),\phi^{-1}(\mathrm{dbl}))<\delta]=o_{\delta}(1) for δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Let ℍδ={z∈ℍ:dist⁡(z,ϕ−1​(dbl))>δ}\mathbb{H}^{\delta}=\{z\in\mathbb{H}:\mathrm{dist}(z,\phi^{-1}(\mathrm{dbl}))>\delta\} and Ωδ=ϕ⁡(ℍδ)\Omega^{\delta}=\phi(\mathbb{H}^{\delta}). In the notation of Lemma 3.8, we say that (Ω′,a′,b′)(\Omega^{\prime},a^{\prime},b^{\prime}) satisfies Property (W) if γ′∩dbl=∅\gamma^{\prime}\cap\mathrm{dbl}=\emptyset a.s. The following lemma ensures that the complement of SLE6\SLE_{6} hulls satisfies Property (W).

Lemma 3.9.

Suppose γ\gamma is a chordal SLE6\SLE_{6} as in Theorem 1.4. Then a.s. there exists no point p∈γp\in\gamma such that γ∖{p}\gamma\setminus\{p\} is disconnected and γ\gamma visits pp at least twice.

4 Minkowski content for percolation pivotal points

This section is devoted to proving Proposition 1.8 and Theorem 1.9.

Recall that SLEκ⁡(ρ)\SLE_{\kappa}(\rho) and SLEκ⁡(ρ1;ρ2)\SLE_{\kappa}(\rho_{1};\rho_{2}) processes are variants of SLEκ\SLE_{\kappa} whose driving functions have forcing terms prescribed by force points with certain weights. SLEκ⁡(ρ)\SLE_{\kappa}(\rho) has a single force point of weight ρ\rho, while SLEκ⁡(ρ1;ρ2)\SLE_{\kappa}(\rho_{1};\rho_{2}) has two force points of weight ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2}, respectively. We will not give the formal definition of these processes and refer instead to [MS16, Section 2.2], because we only use a few well-established facts about the processes developed in the framework of imaginary geometry [MS16].

We also recall the Brownian excursion on ℍ\mathbb{H} from 00 to ∞\infty. See [Law05, Chapter 2] for the precise definition. By the theory of conformal restriction [LSW03] the left and right boundary of the Brownian excursion and those of SLE6⁡(2,2)\SLE_{6}(2;2) have the same law. (In fact, the hull of both Brownian excursion and SLE6⁡(2,2)\SLE_{6}(2,2) are the unique chordal restriction measure with exponent 1.) Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the intersection of the left and right boundaries of the Brownian excursion, i.e. the set of cut points. By [HLLS18, Theorem 4.7], in the notation of Definition 1.2, we have the following.

Lemma 4.1.

The occupation measure of 𝒞\mathcal{C} a.s. exists and is defined by its 3/43/4-dimensional Minkowski content.

Remark 4.2.

In [HLLS18, Theorem 4.7], the notion of a cut point is defined via cut times. Namely, given a Brownian excursion (E⁡(t))t≥0(E(t))_{t\geq 0} on ℍ\mathbb{H} from 0 to ∞\infty, the set of cut points of EE is defined by 𝒞′={η⁡(t):t≥0​and⁡E⁡((0,t))∩E⁡((t,∞))=∅}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\{\eta(t)\,:\,t\geq 0\operatorname{\,\,and\,\,}E((0,t))\cap E((t,\infty))=\emptyset\}. However, it can be checked that 𝒞′=𝒞\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C} a.s. The direction 𝒞′⊂𝒞\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{C} a.s. is trivial. For the other direction, let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the hull of EE, which has the same law as the hull of SLE6⁡(2,2)\SLE_{6}(2,2). By the SLE duality, the interior of ℋ\mathcal{H} is a countable collection of simply connected open sets, ordered by the order in which they are first visited if we go from 0 to ∞\infty inside ℋ\mathcal{H}. In particular, for each p∈𝒞p\in\mathcal{C}, 𝒞∖{p}\mathcal{C}\setminus\{p\} has two components, one bounded and one unbounded, such that all the sets in the bounded component are ordered before the sets in the unbounded component. Suppose there exists p∈𝒞∖𝒞′p\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}^{\prime}. Let 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} be the bounded and unbounded component of 𝒞∖{p}\mathcal{C}\setminus\{p\}, respectively. Let t1t_{1} be the first time E⁡(t)=pE(t)=p and q∈E⁡((0,t1))∩E⁡((t1,∞))q\in E((0,t_{1}))\cap E((t_{1},\infty)). Then q∈𝒞1q\in\mathcal{C}_{1} and there exists t′>t1t^{\prime}>t_{1} such that E⁡(t′)=qE(t^{\prime})=q. For a rational s∈(t1,t′)s\in(t_{1},t^{\prime}), E⁡(s)E(s) a.s. is contained in a component BB of the interior of ℋ\mathcal{H}. Moreover, the closure of BB only has two points in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, one of which must be visited by EE twice. Since there are only countably many such points, this can be ruled out by the strong Markov property of EE and the fact that a planar Brownian motion a.s. does not visit any fixed point. This gives 𝒞⊂𝒞′\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{C}^{\prime} a.s.

Run an SLE8/3(2;−4/3)\SLE_{8/3}(2;-4/3) on (ℍ,0,∞)(\mathbb{H},0,\infty) where the force points are at 0−0^{-} and 0+0^{+}. Conditioning on this curve, run an SLE8/3(−4/3;4/3)\SLE_{8/3}(-4/3;4/3) on the domain to its left. Let ℍ′⊂ℍ\mathbb{H}^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{H} be the domain between these two curves. Conditioning on ℍ′\mathbb{H}^{\prime}, we run an SLE6⁡(1,1)\SLE_{6}(1;1) on (ℍ′,0,∞)(\mathbb{H}^{\prime},0,\infty). Then by the rule of interacting flow lines in [MS16], the marginal law of this curve is an SLE6⁡(2,2)\SLE_{6}(2;2) on (ℍ,0,∞)(\mathbb{H},0,\infty) with force points at 0+0^{+} and 0−0^{-}. See the left part of Figure 2 for an illustration.

Let Υ1\Upsilon^{1} be an SLE6⁡(2)\SLE_{6}(2) on (ℍ,0,∞)(\mathbb{H},0,\infty) where the single force point is at 0+0^{+}. Then Υ1∩ℝ>0=∅\Upsilon^{1}\cap\mathbb{R}_{>0}=\emptyset. Now conditioning on Υ1\Upsilon^{1}, let Υ2\Upsilon^{2} be a chordal SLE6\SLE_{6} from 00 to ∞\infty on the domain to the right of Υ1\Upsilon^{1}. By SLE\SLE duality (see [Zha08, Theorem 5.1] and [MS16, Theorem 1.4]) the right boundary of Υ1\Upsilon^{1} and the left boundary of Υ2\Upsilon^{2} have the same joint law as the left and right boundary of an SLE6⁡(1,1)\SLE_{6}(1,1). See the right part of Figure 2 for an illustration. Denote their intersection by 𝒫¯\overline{\mathcal{P}}. Combined with the paragraph above, we have the following.

Lemma 4.3.

There is a coupling of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℍ′\mathbb{H}^{\prime}, and 𝒫¯\overline{\mathcal{P}} such that 𝒫¯\overline{\mathcal{P}} is independent of ℍ′\mathbb{H}^{\prime}, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the image of 𝒫¯\overline{\mathcal{P}} under a conformal map from ℍ\mathbb{H} to ℍ′\mathbb{H}^{\prime} fixing 00 and ∞\infty.

The next lemma links 𝒫¯\overline{\mathcal{P}} to the set 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Proposition 1.8 and Theorem 1.9.

Lemma 4.4.

Recall (Ω,a,b,c,d)(\Omega,a,b,c,d) and γ1,γ2\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2} in Theorem 1.7. Let γ¯2\overline{\gamma}^{2} be the time-reversal of γ2\gamma^{2}. There exist random times σ\sigma and τ\tau for Υ1\Upsilon^{1} satisfying 0<σ<τ<∞0<\sigma<\tau<\infty with positive probability, such that the following hold on the event that 0<σ<τ<∞0<\sigma<\tau<\infty.

  1. 1.

    The unbounded component of ℍ∖(Υ1​([0,σ])∪Υ1​([τ,∞])CLOSE\mathbb{H}\setminus(\Upsilon^{1}([0,\sigma])\cup\Upsilon^{1}([\tau,\infty]) can be conformally mapped to Ω\Omega with (Υ1​(σ),0,∞,Υ1​(τ))(\Upsilon^{1}(\sigma),0,\infty,\Upsilon^{1}(\tau)) mapped to (a,b,c,d)(a,b,c,d).

  2. 2.

    Conditioning on the realization of ℍ∖(Υ1​([0,σ])∪Υ1​([τ,∞])CLOSE\mathbb{H}\setminus(\Upsilon^{1}([0,\sigma])\cup\Upsilon^{1}([\tau,\infty]), the joint law of the conformal image of Υ1​([σ,τ])\Upsilon^{1}([\sigma,\tau]) and Υ2\Upsilon^{2} is the same as the conditional law of (γ1,γ¯2)(\gamma^{1},\overline{\gamma}^{2}) conditioning on EcE^{c}.

Proof.

Let tt be the last time where Im⁡(Υ1)=1\operatorname{Im}(\Upsilon^{1})=1. By [MW17, Lemma 2.2], Υ1​[0,t]\Upsilon^{1}[0,t] stays close to any deterministic smooth curve in ℍ\mathbb{H} from the origin to a point on {z:Im⁡z=1}\{z:\operatorname{Im}z=1\} with positive probability. Therefore, with positive probability Υ1\Upsilon^{1} reaches a time s<ts<t when Condition 1 in Lemma 4.4 is achieved with s,ts,t in place of σ,τ\sigma,\tau. On the event that there is such a time s∈(0,t)s\in(0,t), let σ\sigma be the infimum of such times. Note that σ>0\sigma>0 a.s. since as s→0s\to 0 the extremal distance between the arc from Υ1​(s)\Upsilon^{1}(s) to 00 and the arc from ∞\infty to Υ1​(τ)\Upsilon^{1}(\tau) in the unbounded component of ℍ∖(Υ1​([0,s])∪Υ1​([τ,∞]))\mathbb{H}\setminus(\Upsilon^{1}([0,s])\cup\Upsilon^{1}([\tau,\infty])) goes to zero. We set σ=∞\sigma=\infty if this event does not occur and let τ=t∨σ\tau=t\vee\sigma.

Viewing Υ1,Υ2\Upsilon^{1},\Upsilon^{2} as two counterflow lines of different angles in the same imaginary geometry ([MS16]), for i=1,2i=1,2, conditioning on Υi\Upsilon^{i}, the law of Υ3−i\Upsilon^{3-i} is a chordal SLE6\SLE_{6}. Therefore the domain Markov property and reversibility of SLE6\SLE_{6} yield that the same resampling property holds for the conformal image of Υ1​([σ,τ])\Upsilon^{1}([\sigma,\tau]) and Υ2\Upsilon^{2}. By convergence of (γη1,γη2)(\gamma^{1}_{\eta},\gamma^{2}_{\eta}) to (γ1,γ2)(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}), the same resampling property holds for (γ1,γ¯2)(\gamma^{1},\overline{\gamma}^{2}) conditioning on EcE^{c}. As explained in [MSW16, Appendix A], this resampling property uniquely determines the law of the pair of curves. Thus we conclude the proof. ∎

Combining Lemmas 4.1, 4.3, and 4.4, we see that on the event EcE^{c} the occupation measure of 𝒫\mathcal{P} exists and is defined by its 3/43/4-dimensional Minkowski content. The same argument works when conditioning on EE. This gives Proposition 1.8.

The proof of Theorem 1.9 follows from the exact same argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.6. We just need to replace one interface γ\gamma with the pair of interfaces γ1,γ2\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}. Here we only point out the substitutes of the ingredients in the argument in Section 3.

Suppose we are in the coupling of Theorems 1.7 and 2.1. Then Lemma 2.7 and the 4-arm case of Lemma 2.8 and (7) give the analog of Lemmas 3.3, 3.4, and  3.5, in addition to (13). We can also adapt the concept of face in this setting, where the number of arcs becomes 4 instead of 2. We use the same notations as in Section 2.5. Given ℬ\mathcal{B}, let 𝒜(ℬ,Ω)={𝒫∩ℬ≠∅}\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{B},\Omega)=\{\mathcal{P}\cap\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset\}. On the event 𝒜⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{B},\Omega), we trace γ1\gamma^{1} and γ2\gamma^{2} and their time-reversals from a,b,c,da,b,c,d until first hitting ℬ\mathcal{B}. This defines a face at Θ\Theta at ℬ\mathcal{B} induced by (γ1,γ2)(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}). Moreover, 𝒟⁡(ℬ,Ω)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{B},\Omega) and 𝒢Ω​(ℬ,U)\mathcal{G}_{\Omega}(\mathcal{B},U) can be defined in the same way as in Section 2.5. Then Lemmas 2.9 and 2.10 still hold with k=2,3k=2,3 replaced by k=4,5k=4,5. Now if we carry out the argument in Section 3, Theorem 1.9 will be reduced to the analog of (21), which can still be proved by a coupling argument as in Lemma 3.6 combined with approximation arguments as in Lemmas 3.8, 3.9, and 3.10.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

According to Lemma 5.1, by possibly restricting to a subsequence, we can assume that γ^η\widehat{\gamma}_{\eta} converge a.s. to a curve γ′\gamma^{\prime} in the ρ\rho-metric. Furthermore, we can assume that along this subsequence (τη,γη)(\tau_{\eta},\gamma_{\eta}) converges to (τ,γ)(\tau,\gamma) a.s. in the topology of Theorem 1.5, where γ\gamma is a chordal SLE6\SLE_{6} (viewed as a curve modulo reparametrization of time). It suffices to show that γ′=γ^\gamma^{\prime}=\widehat{\gamma} a.s.

Conditioning on all the data above, we can sample a random time UU uniformly in (0,τ⁡(Ω))(0,\tau(\Omega)) and a random edge eηe_{\eta} according to τη\tau_{\eta} on γη\gamma_{\eta} such that ℙ[γ^η(U)∈eη]≥1−oη(1)\mathbb{P}[\widehat{\gamma}_{\eta}(U)\in e_{\eta}]\geq 1-o_{\eta}(1). Here we identify edges on the hexagonal lattice with their midpoints since the difference is negligible in the scaling limit. On the other hand, since τη\tau_{\eta} converge to τ\tau in the Prokhorov metric a.s., by Lemma 5.3 we have that eηe_{\eta} converges in law to γ^​(U)\widehat{\gamma}(U). This implies that γ′​(U)\gamma^{\prime}(U) and γ^​(U)\widehat{\gamma}(U) are equal in law.

Given any fixed t>0t>0, on the event that t∈(0,τ⁡(Ω))t\in(0,\tau(\Omega)), let AA be the hull of γ^​([0,t])\widehat{\gamma}([0,t]) and Aε={z∈ℂ:dist(z,A))≤ε}A_{\varepsilon}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{dist}(z,A))\leq\varepsilon\}. Since τ⁡(A∖∂A)≤t\tau(A\setminus\partial A)\leq t and (by Theorem 1.6 and Lemma 5.2) τ⁡(∂A)=0\tau(\partial A)=0, we have limε→0τ⁡(Aε)=t\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\tau(A_{\varepsilon})=t. Thus for all δ>0\delta>0 with t+2​δ<τ⁡(Ω)t+2\delta<\tau(\Omega), we can find a (random) ε>0\varepsilon>0 a.s. such that τ⁡(Aε)≤t+δ\tau(A_{\varepsilon})\leq t+\delta. Therefore lim supη→0τη​(Aε)≤t+δ\limsup_{\eta\to 0}\tau_{\eta}(A_{\varepsilon})\leq t+\delta. Hence for sufficiently small η\eta there exists tηδ∈[t,t+2​δ]t^{\delta}_{\eta}\in[t,t+2\delta] such that γ^η​(tηδ)∉Aε\widehat{\gamma}_{\eta}(t^{\delta}_{\eta})\notin A_{\varepsilon}. By possibly passing to a subsequence, we can assume limη→0tηδ→tδ\lim_{\eta\to 0}t^{\delta}_{\eta}\to t^{\delta}. Sending η→0\eta\to 0, we have γ′​(tδ)∉γ^​([0,t])\gamma^{\prime}(t^{\delta})\notin\widehat{\gamma}([0,t]). Since γ′\gamma^{\prime} and γ^\widehat{\gamma} have the same range, we must have γ^​(t)∈γ′​([0,tδ])\widehat{\gamma}(t)\in\gamma^{\prime}([0,t^{\delta}]). Letting δ→0\delta\to 0, we have γ^​(t)∈γ′​([0,t])\widehat{\gamma}(t)\in\gamma^{\prime}([0,t]). By considering rational tt’s and then using the continuity of γ^\widehat{\gamma} and γ′\gamma^{\prime}, we see that a.s. γ^​([0,t])⊂γ′​([0,t])\widehat{\gamma}([0,t])\subset\gamma^{\prime}([0,t]) for all t∈(0,τ⁡(Ω))t\in(0,\tau(\Omega)). Combined with γ′​(U)​=𝑑​γ^​(U)\gamma^{\prime}(U)\overset{d}{=}\widehat{\gamma}(U), we have γ′​(U)=γ^​(U)\gamma^{\prime}(U)=\widehat{\gamma}(U) hence γ′=γ^\gamma^{\prime}=\widehat{\gamma} a.s. ∎
